facts.claim: Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of electromagnetic radiation from their magnetic poles, which are observed as pulses when the beam sweeps past Earth.
facts.verification_notes: This is the standard and well-established definition of pulsars, confirmed by NASA and astrophysics textbooks.

facts.claim: The first pulsar was discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish on November 28, 1967, using the Interplanetary Scintillation Array at the Mullard Radio Astronomy Observatory.
facts.source: Nobel Prize (for Hewish, not Bell Burnell) / Cambridge University
facts.verification_notes: The discovery date and instrument are correct. Bell Burnell was the primary discoverer, but Hewish shared the Nobel Prize with Martin Ryle; both are recognized for their roles.

facts.claim: The fastest known pulsar, PSR J1748-2446ad, rotates at a frequency of 716 times per second, corresponding to a period of 1.396 milliseconds.
facts.verification_notes: This is well-documented in the cited arXiv paper (Hessels et al. 2006) and confirmed by multiple sources. The period 1/716 s = 1.396 ms is accurate.

facts.claim: The first millisecond pulsar, PSR B1937+21, was discovered in 1982 by Donald Backer and colleagues; its period is 1.558 milliseconds.
facts.source: Backer et al., Nature (via NASA HEASARC)
facts.verification_notes: Backer et al. (1982) discovered this pulsar; period of 1.558 ms is correct. Some sources cite 1.5578 ms, but 1.558 is a standard rounded value.

facts.claim: The first pulsar discovered outside the Milky Way galaxy was PSR B0529-66, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, discovered in 1989.
facts.verification_notes: The first extra-Milky-Way pulsar was PSR B0540-69 in the LMC, discovered in 1984 (and confirmed in 1985). PSR B0529-66 is not a known pulsar designation. The ATNF catalogue lists PSR B0540-69 as the first extragalactic pulsar.

facts.claim: The Crab Pulsar (PSR B0531+21) was created by the supernova explosion observed in 1054 AD, and has a rotation period of 33 milliseconds.
facts.verification_notes: The Crab Nebula and pulsar are confirmed remnants of SN 1054. The rotational period is ~33 ms (often cited as 33.5 ms). Accurate.

facts.claim: Pulsars lose rotational energy over time; the Crab Pulsar's spin period increases by about 36 nanoseconds per day due to energy loss via electromagnetic radiation and particle winds.
facts.verification_notes: Jodrell Bank observations give a period derivative of ~4.2e-13 s/s, which translates to ~36 ns/day. This is a well-known value.

facts.claim: The most precise pulsar timing array, the North American Nanohertz Observatory for Gravitational Waves (NANOGrav), announced in June 2023 the detection of a gravitational wave background signal using 68 pulsars over 15 years.
facts.verification_notes: The NANOGrav 15-year data set (published June 2023) used 68 pulsars and reported strong evidence for a gravitational wave background. Correct.

facts.claim: The first exoplanets ever discovered were found around a pulsar, PSR B1257+12, in 1992 by Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail; three planets orbit the pulsar.
facts.verification_notes: Wolszczan and Frail announced the first confirmed exoplanets in 1992 around PSR B1257+12, and subsequently two more planets were confirmed (total 3). Correct.

facts.claim: The fastest pulsar wind nebula jet observed is in the Vela Pulsar, moving at about 70% of the speed of light.
facts.verification_notes: Chandra X-ray observations of the Vela pulsar wind nebula show a jet with apparent velocity of ~0.7c, confirmed by several studies. The claim is accurate.

facts.claim: The typical radius of a neutron star (the parent of a pulsar) is about 10 kilometers, with a mass around 1.4 times the mass of the Sun.
facts.verification_notes: This is standard astrophysical knowledge. Most neutron stars have radii between 9-12 km and masses around 1.4 solar masses (the Chandrasekhar limit).

facts.claim: The surface gravity of a neutron star is approximately 2 x 10^11 times that of Earth (about 2 billion g).
facts.verification_notes: Using g = GM/R², with M=1.4 solar masses and R=10 km, gives ~2e11 m/s², which is about 2e10 times Earth's 9.8 m/s². The claim says 2e11 times Earth's gravity, which is an order of magnitude off. Correct value is ~2e10 times Earth's gravity (2e11 m/s² is the value in SI, not the ratio). So the claim as written is incorrect.

facts.claim: There are over 3,000 known radio pulsars catalogued in the ATNF Pulsar Catalogue as of 2020.
facts.source: Australia Telescope National Facility (ATNF) Pulsar Catalogue
facts.verification_notes: The ATNF catalogue (v1.68) had 2,800+ pulsars by 2020, but by mid-2020 it exceeded 3,000. Many sources confirm >3,000. Accurate.

facts.claim: The first pulsar glitch (sudden spin-up) was observed in the Vela Pulsar in 1969, only a year after its discovery.
facts.verification_notes: The Vela pulsar (discovered 1968) showed a glitch in 1969, reported by Radhakrishnan and Manchester. Correct.

facts.claim: The most massive neutron star known, PSR J0740+6620, has a mass of 2.14 solar masses (with uncertainties of ±0.09), measured using Shapiro delay in 2019.
facts.source: Cromartie et al., Nature Astronomy (via NANOGrav)
facts.verification_notes: Cromartie et al. (2019) reported 2.14 +- 0.09 solar masses using Shapiro delay, and subsequent refined measurements confirm this. At the time, it was the most massive known.

hook_ideas: Start with the audio of a pulsar's radio pulses (beep rhythm) and ask: What cosmic lighthouse is sending this signal?
Imagine the first detection in 1967: Jocelyn Bell noticed a 'scruffy' signal that appeared every 1.337 seconds, briefly nicknamed 'LGM' (Little Green Men) before being identified as a natural source.
Show the spinning neutron star with beams sweeping past Earth, comparing it to a lighthouse beam in the dark ocean.
Use the fact that the fastest pulsar spins 716 times per second — faster than a kitchen blender — to blow your mind.
Pose the question: How can we use pulsars as galactic GPS for future spacecraft? (NASA's NICER mission tested this in 2018.)
misconceptions: Pulsars are not actually pulsing stars; they emit continuous beams that only appear to pulse when the beam crosses our line of sight, like a lighthouse beam (a geometric effect).
Pulsars are not the same as neutron stars; all pulsars are neutron stars, but only a fraction of neutron stars emit beams in our direction and are seen as pulsars.

The first pulsar was not discovered by the Nobel Prize winner Antony Hewish alone; Jocelyn Bell Burnell made the primary observation and was controversially omitted from the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Pulsars do not 'spin down' forever uniformly; they occasionally undergo 'glitches' – sudden increases in rotation speed due to crust-quakes or superfluid interactions.
The beams from pulsars are not composed of visible light only; they range from radio to X-ray and gamma-ray wavelengths.
